newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Oil prices rise, stocks down in Asia on Iraq hit. [CORRECTED 11:34 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rise, stocks down in Asia on Iraq hit. [CORRECTED 11:34 GMT]

text.p: News the U.S. attacked air defense targets in Iraq swept through Asian financial markets on Tuesday, with the most dramatic and immediate impact seen in oil prices which rose sharply higher.
Share prices fell sharply in some centers, while the dollar rose and gold inched slightly higher.
The key Brent futures contract traded on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) jumped to $23.50 after opening at $22.90.

In Tokyo, a senior economist at the Japanese Institute of Middle Eastern Economies, Kazuaki Kondo, predicted the price of light crude oil traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange-- another key price barometer-- could soar to $30.
He did not give a time frame within which it may happen.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index dropped sharply in response to the news and later was down 1.35 percent at 10,957.18.

"This is a kneejerk reaction to something we really have no control over," Anthony Edwards, a director at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, (corrects spelling of company name) in Hong Kong said of the stock market there.
The Pentegon announced the U.S. military launched cruise missile strikes against targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds.
"It should not (have a lasting impact on the market,") Barkley's Edwards said.
But he said traders must remain cautious because of the impact there could be on commodities markets if the situation is protracted. "Then that is a concern," he added.
Michael Hung, research manager of Nikko Securities in Taiwan said he expects that market to fall further on Wednesday after Tuesday's 1.33 percent drop.
"What worries people most are the potential rises in domestic oil prices and inflation.
"But if war breaks out, I think the United States will end it as soon as possible, so the consequences will not be as great as in the Gulf War," he added.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who has been campaigning for relection, was due to make a statement on the retaliatory strike against Iraq about 1200 gmt.
News of the attacks came just as the Tokyo's Nikkei 225-share index ended with a modest gain.
"The market could not digest the news before the close," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy manager of Nomura Securities Co.
"To the extent that it's going to affect Wall Street, Philippine stocks will also be affected," Raul Ruiz, research head at Sun Hung Kai Securities in Manila said.
Before news of the attacks, market sentiment was dominated by Wall Street's decline last week on fears of a U.S. rate hike.
Concern over U.S. interest rates had intensified because of a report in Tuesday's Wall Street Journal.
The report said the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates by half a percentage point, twice what markets now expect, if upcoming economic data suggests the economy is overheating.
U.S. markets were closed Monday for the Labor Day holiday, and Asian markets are nervously awaiting key economic data.
This includes the latest report by the National Association of Purchasing Managers on Tuesday as well as Friday's key U.S. employment data for August.
Talk of higher interest rates, combined with the attacks on Iraq, pushed the U.S. dollar to a high of 109.35 in Tokyo, before it eased to 109.25 against 109.16 in Europe overnight.
The price of gold in Hong Kong firmed minutes after the strikes were launched and was quoted at US$387.20/387.50 an ounce at 0630 gmt, up from US$386.70/387.20 an ounce earlier.
